[USER] User asked about the difference between Orthodox and Reform Judaism.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox Judaism refers to the traditional form of Judaism that adheres to the strict interpretation of Jewish law and practices.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox Jews believe that Jewish law is divinely inspired and must be followed strictly.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox communities tend to be more insular and conservative, prioritizing preserving traditional practices and beliefs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Judaism is a more progressive form of Judaism that emphasizes individual autonomy and personal interpretation of Jewish law and tradition.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Jews prioritize social justice and ethical values, and tend to be more inclusive and welcoming of diverse backgrounds and beliefs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The main difference between Orthodox and Reform Judaism is the degree to which they adhere to traditional Jewish laws and practices.  
[USER] User inquired about how the differences between Orthodox and Reform Judaism impact daily life and religious practices within each community.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox Jews have a more strict and structured approach to religious practices, following traditional practices such as observing Shabbat and adhering to dietary laws (Kashrut).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox Jews typically have gender-segregated prayer services and require men to wear kippot (yarmulkes) and prayer shawls.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Jews have a more flexible approach to religious practices, often modifying traditional practices according to contemporary values and beliefs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Jews may have mixed-gender prayer services or use musical instruments during worship, which is not traditionally permitted in Orthodox synagogues.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox communities tend to be more insular, emphasizing the importance of maintaining Jewish identity within their own community.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Jews are more open to integrating and interacting with non-Jewish communities and may attend secular schools/universities.  
[USER] User asked if Orthodox and Reform Jews have different beliefs about the afterlife.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Orthodox Judaism believes in an afterlife where the soul is judged for its actions during life, with a positive outcome for those who follow Jewish law.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The afterlife in Orthodox belief includes concepts of heaven (Olam Habah) and punishment (Gehenna).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Reform Judaism does not have a uniform belief in the afterlife, viewing it as more symbolic and focusing on actions in this life.
